title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Animal-production applications include growth, feed efficiency, meat/milk quantity and quality, reproductive performance, health, environmental adaptation and methane. A molecular profile is useful only in relation to a defined question, decision, population and measurement cost. A statistically associated feature may add little predictive value; a predictor may work without identifying a causal mechanism.
An integrated study should specify the primary phenotype and units, experimental unit, target population, exposure, tissue/time, eligible assays, covariates, data processing, missingness and validation. Explain why each molecular layer is needed. A diet-intervention study and a breeding-value prediction study involve different causal and genetic objectives even if both record performance.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For a prediction comparison, calculate the same loss on the same held-out animals for a baseline and an augmented model. If errors are \(e_{i0}\) and \(e_{i1}\), the paired improvement in squared error is \(d_i=e_{i0}^2-e_{i1}^2\). Its mean is positive when the augmented model has smaller mean squared error in that group.
One evaluation set gives conditional evidence, not a universal benefit. Costs, feasibility, calibration, independent replication and relevance to selection or management still need assessment.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
observed <- c(10,12,9,14,11,13)
baseline <- c(11,11,11,11,11,11)
augmented <- c(10.5,11.7,9.5,13.4,11.2,12.7)
d <- (observed-baseline)^2-(observed-augmented)^2
c(baseline_RMSE=sqrt(mean((observed-baseline)^2)),
 augmented_RMSE=sqrt(mean((observed-augmented)^2)),
 paired_MSE_improvement=mean(d))


         baseline_RMSE         augmented_RMSE paired_MSE_improvement 
             1.7795130              0.4242641              2.9866667 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(mean(d)-(mean((observed-baseline)^2)-mean((observed-augmented)^2)))<1e-12)


The supplied predictions improve squared-error loss for these six fictional animals. The calculation says nothing about how those predictions were trained or whether they generalize.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Follow-up can include replication in a new farm, time, breed or management setting; a targeted assay or perturbation can address a mechanistic question. Choose follow-up to resolve the uncertainty actually present, not merely to generate more molecular measurements.

title: Animal-production questions and integrated reporting
text:
5. Exercises

Why compare predictions on the same test animals?
Does predictive improvement show that an assay measures a causal mediator?
What belongs in a concise final report?







Suggested answers






It makes the comparison paired and avoids changing the population between models.
No; proxies can predict through correlation.
Question, design, data and exclusions, model, validation, numerical evidence, limitations and justified next step.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Single-cell assays can resolve molecular differences across sampled cells, but cells are nested within specimens and animals. Treatment allocation to an animal does not create independent treatment allocations to every sampled cell. Cell recovery and QC affect the representation of cell types. For an animal-level comparison, one approach aggregates measurements by animal and cell type before using an appropriate sample-level analysis; this still requires biological replication.
Spatial assays retain positional information at a platform-dependent resolution. Spots can mix cells, adjacent positions can be dependent, and resolution varies. Chromatin conformation assays estimate selected contact relationships, not a deterministic map of regulatory causation. Advanced epigenomic measurements retain their assay-specific limitations.
AI models can learn useful patterns, but a sophisticated architecture does not eliminate sample dependence, leakage or confounding. A generated explanation is not supporting biological evidence. Specify training data, evaluation units, uncertainty and validation context.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For m cells per animal with equal marginal variance \(\sigma^2\) and within-animal correlation rho, a design-effect approximation is \(D=1+(m-1)\rho\). Treating \(nm\) cells as independent can overstate precision; \(nm/D\) is an effective-count illustration under this equal-correlation model, not a replacement for a valid hierarchical analysis or degrees of freedom.
For high-dimensional prediction, keep animals or specimens separated across training and evaluation when that represents the intended task.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
animals <- 6; cells <- 100; rho <- .1
design_effect <- 1+(cells-1)*rho
c(raw_cell_count=animals*cells,
 equal_correlation_effective_count=animals*cells/design_effect,
 independent_animals=animals)


                   raw_cell_count equal_correlation_effective_count 
                        600.00000                          55.04587 
              independent_animals 
                          6.00000 


Show R code
set.seed(1601)
cell <- data.frame(animal=rep(paste0("a",1:6),each=10),
 value=rep(rnorm(6),each=10)+rnorm(60,sd=.2))
aggregate(value~animal,cell,mean)


  animal      value
1     a1 -2.2732628
2     a2 -1.2333922
3     a3 -1.1853579
4     a4 -0.1604756
5     a5 -1.4696498
6     a6  0.5503939


The example retains six animals despite measuring many cells. The effective-count approximation is a description of variance inflation in a stylised model, not permission to conduct inference with an invented sample size.

title: Single-cell, spatial and emerging methods
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Evaluate cell-type annotation, recovery, doublets, QC, spatial scale and biological replication. Method-specific pipelines and validations are needed before a real analysis. Advanced extensions in this course critique supplied designs and evidence; they do not claim to implement single-cell or spatial software workflows.

Why is splitting cells from each animal across train and test unsafe for new-animal prediction?
What can a spatial co-location establish?
What evidence should support an AI-derived candidate?







Suggested answers






The model can learn animal-specific patterns present in both sets.
Proximity at the assay’s resolution, not necessarily molecular interaction.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text: Define eligible backgrounds and selection rules; calculate enrichment under a supplied null; construct and interpret networks with explicit edge definitions.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A pathway analysis asks whether selected features are represented in a gene set more than expected under a specified model. Define the eligible background from genes that could have been selected, not every annotated gene regardless of assay coverage. Selection can depend on abundance, length, missingness or mapping, which can violate equal-selection assumptions.
A network represents entities as nodes and a defined relationship as edges. A correlation network, protein-interaction database and curated metabolic network have different edge meanings. A dense cluster can reflect a common driver, duplicated measurements or technical structure. Gene regulation involves direction and mechanism; undirected correlation alone supplies neither.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
2. Model and assumptions
With N eligible genes, K in a pathway and n selected genes, the hypergeometric null assumes a uniformly selected subset of size n. For overlap x, the enrichment tail is \(P(X\ge x)\) under \(X\sim Hypergeometric(N,K,n)\). If pathway tests are numerous, address multiplicity.
For a binary undirected adjacency matrix A with zero diagonal, degree is \(d_i=\sum_j A_{ij}\). It describes connectivity under the selected definition and threshold, not an intrinsic universal importance of the gene.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
N <- 100; K <- 20; n <- 10; x <- 5
p <- phyper(x-1,K,N-K,n,lower.tail=FALSE)
c(expected_overlap=n*K/N,observed_overlap=x,enrichment_p=p)


expected_overlap observed_overlap     enrichment_p 
      2.00000000       5.00000000       0.02546455 


Show R code
A <- matrix(c(0,1,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1,0),4,4,byrow=TRUE)
dimnames(A) <- list(paste0("g",1:4),paste0("g",1:4))
stopifnot(isSymmetric(A),all(diag(A)==0),sum(A)==2*4)
rowSums(A)


g1 g2 g3 g4 
 2  2  3  1 


The expected overlap is two under the supplied background and sampling rule. Degree depends on the four chosen nodes and their edges. These are fictional pathways and networks.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Overlapping gene sets and correlated gene statistics complicate enrichment inference. Report membership/version, mapping, background, selection rule and adjustment. Network robustness requires resampling or independent validation; causality requires stronger design or assumptions than correlation.

title: Pathway enrichment and biological networks
text:
5. Exercises

Why can a genome-wide background be inappropriate for a protein assay?
Does an enrichment p-value measure pathway activity?
What changes when a correlation threshold is raised?







Suggested answers






Many genes could not have been observed or selected.
No; it concerns representation under a null, not direct activity.
Edges and node degrees can change, showing their dependence on the supplied rule.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text: Distinguish inference and prediction; evaluate multiple testing, regularization and dimensionality reduction; prevent preprocessing and repeated-animal leakage.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
High-dimensional assays contain correlated features, different scales and substantial measurement variation. More variables can improve a model, but can also overfit a small sample. Regression requires a stated response, experimental unit, design and assumptions. Clustering and principal components describe patterns; they do not prove biological mechanisms.
Inference estimates an effect and its uncertainty under a model. Prediction evaluates performance for the intended new population. A split between rows can be inadequate if records from the same animal, family, farm or time series appear in both sets. The validation group should represent the deployment task, and preprocessing must be fitted using training data only.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For standardised training features X and centred response y, ridge regression minimises \(\|y-X\beta\|^2+\lambda \|\beta\|^2\), giving \(\widehat\beta=(X^T X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty\). A positive lambda shrinks coefficients; choose it using training-only validation, not test outcomes. The intercept is handled separately.
Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment addresses false-discovery-rate control under its applicable dependence conditions. An adjusted p-value is not the probability that an individual hypothesis is false.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1201)
X <- matrix(rnorm(30*4),30,4)
y <- 1+X[,1]-.5*X[,2]+rnorm(30)
train <- 1:20; test <- 21:30
center <- colMeans(X[train,]); scale_train <- apply(X[train,],2,sd)
Ztrain <- scale(X[train,],center,scale_train)
Ztest <- scale(X[test,],center,scale_train)
ybar <- mean(y[train]); lambda <- 2 # Supplied, not tuned on the test set.
beta <- solve(crossprod(Ztrain)+lambda*diag(4),crossprod(Ztrain,y[train]-ybar))
prediction <- as.vector(ybar+Ztest%*%beta)
c(test_RMSE=sqrt(mean((y[test]-prediction)^2)),
 baseline_RMSE=sqrt(mean((y[test]-ybar)^2)))


    test_RMSE baseline_RMSE 
     1.055431      1.539884 


Show R code
p.adjust(c(.001,.02,.04,.4),method="BH")


[1] 0.00400000 0.04000000 0.05333333 0.40000000


The test rows affect neither scaling nor coefficients. One split illustrates the process; its performance is not a stable estimate for a livestock population.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Use appropriate loss and uncertainty, inspect residuals and state model-selection decisions. Screening features on all outcomes before splitting leaks information even if the final model is fitted on training rows. A penalty value selected on the test set turns it into a tuning set. The association practical (in development) distinguishes marker evidence from validated prediction.

title: Statistical models and honest validation
text:
5. Exercises

Why reuse training means for test scaling?
Can test RMSE be used to choose lambda and still be an untouched test score?
Does a PCA cluster establish a treatment effect?







Suggested answers






The deployment transformation must not depend on the new group’s distribution.
No; use a separate validation procedure within training, then evaluate once on test data.
No; batches, other covariates and sampling can also create clusters.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text: Distinguish amplicon and metagenomic measurements; explain compositionality; evaluate host–microbiome associations and sampling limitations.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A microbiome sample measures a community at a particular site, time and collection process. Amplicon data focus on selected marker sequences; shotgun metagenomics samples broader sequence content. Sequence representation depends on extraction, library preparation, genome properties and reference annotation. A taxonomic abundance profile does not directly measure metabolic activity.
Rumen, intestinal and faecal samples answer different questions. Host diet, genotype, management and physiology can influence the community while also influencing a production trait. Association between a taxon and methane, for example, can arise from those shared drivers; it does not demonstrate that changing the taxon would change emissions.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
2. Model and assumptions
Relative abundance is \(p_{ij}=x_{ij}/\sum_k x_{kj}\). Because the components sum to one, increasing one absolute component can reduce the relative representation of another whose absolute amount did not change.
For strictly positive components, a log ratio \(\log(x_A/x_B)\) is invariant to a common sample multiplier. Zero handling needs an explicit measurement assumption: adding an arbitrary constant can alter conclusions, especially for rare taxa.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
absolute <- rbind(before=c(A=10,B=10,C=10),after=c(A=20,B=10,C=10))
relative <- absolute/rowSums(absolute)
relative


               A         B         C
before 0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333
after  0.5000000 0.2500000 0.2500000


Show R code
c(B_absolute_change=absolute[2,"B"]-absolute[1,"B"],
 B_relative_change=relative[2,"B"]-relative[1,"B"])


B_absolute_change B_relative_change 
       0.00000000       -0.08333333 


Show R code
stopifnot(absolute[2,"B"]==absolute[1,"B"],relative[2,"B"]<relative[1,"B"])
log(absolute[,"A"]/absolute[,"B"])


   before     after 
0.0000000 0.6931472 


B becomes a smaller fraction even though its absolute amount is unchanged. A change in total microbial load is not observable from these fractions alone.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Distinguish microbial load, relative composition, genetic potential and activity. Consider contaminants, reference coverage, repeated measurements, host-level confounding and independent validation. Host–microbiome co-metabolism is a mechanistic hypothesis to examine with appropriate molecular and experimental evidence.

title: Microbial communities and host relationships
text:
5. Exercises

Which taxon changed absolute amount?
Can relative B alone establish that B was depleted?
What extra measurement could inform total microbial load?







Suggested answers






A doubled.
No; its fraction decreased through the change in A.
A justified absolute-quantification measurement, such as calibrated load estimates, with its own sampling and technical assumptions.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text: Distinguish peptide evidence, protein-group inference and abundance; evaluate missing values and transformations; interpret structural information without overclaiming function.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Proteomics can quantify molecular evidence from peptides or proteins using platforms such as mass spectrometry. A measured peptide may be shared by multiple proteins; assigning it to a unique gene product is an inference problem. Identification confidence and abundance uncertainty are separate. Sample preparation, digestion, instrument response and batch effects influence measured values.
A protein table can contain missing values because abundance is low, a feature was not identified or processing failed. These mechanisms imply different analysis choices. Replacing every missing value by zero treats non-observation as a known measurement and can introduce artificial group differences. On a log scale, zero is not an absence: it represents an original-scale value of one.
Structural records describe coordinates of a measured or predicted molecular model. A geometrical contact suggests spatial proximity within that model; it does not alone establish biochemical interaction or functional importance.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
2. Model and assumptions
If \(z=\log_2(x)\) for positive abundance x, a difference \(z_T-z_C\) corresponds to a ratio \(2^{z_T-z_C}\). The example compares arithmetic means of log2 measurements, so the ratio corresponds to geometric means on the original scale.
Complete-case comparisons require recording which values remain in each group. They can be biased when observation depends on abundance or group.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
z <- c(8,8.5,NA,9,9.2,NA)
group <- factor(c("C","C","C","T","T","T"))
means <- tapply(z,group,mean,na.rm=TRUE)
observed <- tapply(!is.na(z),group,sum)
data.frame(group=names(means),observed=as.vector(observed),mean_log2=as.vector(means))


  group observed mean_log2
1     C        2      8.25
2     T        2      9.10


Show R code
c(log2_difference=means["T"]-means["C"],
 geometric_mean_ratio=2^(means["T"]-means["C"]))


     log2_difference.T geometric_mean_ratio.T 
              0.850000               1.802501 


Both groups retain two measurements. The numerical ratio describes the observed log2 values, not a verified biological treatment effect.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
The teaching protein values are supplied log2 abundances. They are not raw spectra and do not implement peptide identification or protein inference. Report platform, processing, quantification scale, identification thresholds and missingness. Protein structure and abundance answer different questions.

title: Protein identification, abundance and structure
text:
5. Exercises

What ratio corresponds to a log2 difference of one?
Why might low-value imputation strengthen a spurious difference?
Does a close residue pair establish an interaction in a living animal?







Suggested answers






Two.
If one group has more missing values, the imputation can manufacture a lower group mean; its assumptions need justification.
No; context, structural uncertainty and biological evidence are required.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text: Connect RNA counts to biological samples and library exposure; distinguish normalization, visualization and differential-expression inference; interpret model contrasts and dispersion.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Bulk RNA-seq measures RNA from a mixture of cells in a sampled tissue. Read counts depend on abundance, sequencing depth, transcript properties and processing. A difference can arise from expression within a cell type, a change in cell composition, technical effects or combinations of these. Biological replicates are independent experimental units, not reads or genes.
Prepare count matrices and sample metadata with matching IDs. Inspect library sizes and count distributions, define low-information filters independently of a desired direction, and specify the biological contrast and adjustment factors before testing. Expression transformations for visualization are not substitutes for an inferential count model.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A negative-binomial model can write \(K_{gj}\sim NB(\mu_{gj},\alpha_g)\) with \(E[K]=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(K)=\mu+\alpha_g \mu^2\). A known exposure \(s_j\) enters through \(\mu_{gj}=s_j q_{gj}\). Gene-level models describe \(q\) using treatment and other design terms. Dispersion describes extra variation beyond a Poisson model.
The worked calculation uses supplied exposure, not an estimated RNA-seq normalization method. On real data, composition-aware normalization, dispersion estimation, model design and multiplicity require an appropriate workflow.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
mu <- c(10,100,1000)
alpha <- .1
data.frame(mean=mu,Poisson_variance=mu,NB_variance=mu+alpha*mu^2)


  mean Poisson_variance NB_variance
1   10               10          20
2  100              100        1100
3 1000             1000      101000


Show R code
counts <- c(80,120,160)
exposure <- c(.8,1.2,1.6)
normalized <- counts/exposure
normalized


[1] 100 100 100


Show R code
stopifnot(all(normalized==100))


Equal normalized counts can arise from different read depths. At high mean, the overdispersion term dominates Poisson variance; treating biological count data as Poisson can underestimate uncertainty.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
CPM and log2(count+1) are useful teaching transformations but have composition and low-count limitations. The DESeq2 vignette describes a full gene-level count-model workflow. Our base-R practical explores supplied exposure and a restricted quasi-Poisson model; it is not a replacement for its dispersion and normalization framework.

title: Transcriptomics and expression analysis
text:
5. Exercises

Why are genes not independent biological replicates of a treatment?
What happens to raw counts when exposure doubles but abundance is unchanged?
Can a log-count plot prove differential expression?







Suggested answers






Treatment was assigned to animals or other experimental units, not separately to genes.
Their expected counts double.
No; inference needs a specified model, replication, uncertainty and appropriate multiple-testing treatment.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text: Import and join tables by explicit keys; preserve feature/sample orientation; detect missing, duplicated and reordered records; distinguish source data from derived output.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A reproducible script specifies inputs, transformations, analysis and outputs. Begin by deciding which dimension contains features and which contains samples. In this course assay matrices have features in rows and animals in columns; genotype matrices have animals in rows. Metadata has one row per animal. These choices must be checked every time an object is transformed.
Use stable keys, not row position, to align data. Keep raw records separate from derived tables. Record transformations and exclusions. Relative paths within an RStudio project make examples portable; temporary files should stay in temporary directories. R is the main environment. Command-line and Python exercises introduce portable concepts without making them dependencies of every practical.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
2. Model and assumptions
Suppose an assay column is labelled \(a_j\) and metadata row i has animal ID \(m_i\). Alignment is the explicit index \(j_i=\mathrm{match}(m_i,a)\), followed by reordering and an identity check. A missing index means that animal has no matching measurement. Duplicate keys make the mapping ambiguous.
A successful join does not establish that labels are biologically correct. Identity tracking during collection is still necessary.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
metadata <- data.frame(animal=c("a1","a2","a3"), diet=c("C","T","C"))
assay <- matrix(1:6,2,3,dimnames=list(c("f1","f2"),c("a3","a1","a2")))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(metadata$animal), !anyDuplicated(colnames(assay)))
index <- match(metadata$animal,colnames(assay))
stopifnot(!anyNA(index))
aligned <- assay[,index,drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(aligned),metadata$animal))
aligned


   a1 a2 a3
f1  3  5  1
f2  4  6  2


Animal a1 now receives its labelled measurement, not the value in the original first column. Keeping drop=FALSE preserves matrix shape when selecting a single column.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Checking dimensions alone misses permutations. A seed records a simulation draw, but software versions, inputs, processing choices and model assumptions also affect reproducibility. ID checks cannot detect a correctly labelled tube containing the wrong biological specimen.

title: Programming and reproducible data handling
text:

Why is cbind(metadata, t(assay)) unsafe before alignment?
What does match return for an absent animal?
Why should raw and transformed matrices have different names?







Suggested answers






It binds by position and can attach measurements to the wrong animals.
NA; require an explicit missing-sample policy before continuing.
Names preserve which units and transformations each object represents, reducing accidental reuse of a processed value as raw data.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text: Define experimental units and independent replication; distinguish randomisation, blocking and batch adjustment; identify confounded designs and specify sample handling.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text: Define experimental units and independent replication; distinguish randomisation, blocking and batch adjustment; identify confounded designs and specify sample handling.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
For an individually allocated diet, the animal can be the experimental unit. If a diet is allocated to pens, animals within a pen are not independent diet allocations: the pen is the unit for the intervention. Sequencing lanes, aliquots and repeated measurements are technical or within-unit observations, not additional biological replicates.
A multi-omics study should connect animal identity to tissue, collection time, storage, extraction, assay and batch. Collection and preservation requirements differ across molecules; a shared animal identifier does not imply that one preparation is appropriate for every assay. Predefine exclusion rules and the primary contrast. Where possible, randomise treatment allocation, blind handling and distribute biological groups across processing batches.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A simple fixed-effect model is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_T T_i+\beta_B B_i+e_i\). Its design matrix X must have independent columns to separate treatment and batch. If every control is in batch A and every treatment in batch B, the two effects are not separately identifiable. Increasing the number of observations in the same confounded arrangement does not solve this.
Blocking balances treatments within a known nuisance factor; batch adjustment models remaining variation. Neither creates the missing comparisons in a perfectly confounded design.

title: Experimental design and biological sampling
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
balanced <- data.frame(treatment=factor(rep(c("control","treated"),4)),
 batch=factor(rep(c("A","A","B","B"),2)))
confounded <- transform(balanced, batch=treatment)
rank_info <- function(d) {
 X <- model.matrix(~ treatment + batch, d)
 c(columns=ncol(X), rank=qr(X)$rank)
}
rbind(balanced=rank_info(balanced), confounded=rank_info(confounded))


           columns rank
balanced         3    3
confounded       3    2


Show R code
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(~treatment+batch, balanced))$rank==3,
          qr(model.matrix(~treatment+batch, confounded))$rank==2)


The balanced design supplies independent treatment and batch columns. The confounded model has three columns but only rank two: software cannot recover the absent information.

4. Interpretation and scope
Rank is necessary, not sufficient, for a good experiment. Power, within-unit dependence, transport/storage effects, selection and missingness still matter. Plan biological replication using a relevant effect size and variance, not a universal sample-count rule. See the NC3Rs experimental-unit guidance for examples.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A study of feed efficiency can ask whether a diet changes animal performance, whether molecular profiles predict later performance, or which biological mechanisms mediate a change. These questions require different designs. A response to an allocated diet is an intervention contrast; association of a protein with performance is an observational relationship; prediction asks how well a model performs for new animals.
Genomics records sequence variation, transcriptomics records RNA abundance, proteomics records proteins, metabolomics records small molecules, microbiomics describes microbial communities, and phenomics describes traits measured across animals and time. Epigenomic assays describe selected regulatory measurements. Each layer samples a tissue, time and measurement process. A genotype need not predict a transcript in every tissue, and transcript abundance need not determine protein abundance.
Begin with the animal, the exposure, the sampling unit and the decision. Measuring more layers does not compensate for a poorly specified question.

title: Biological questions and omics measurements
text:
2. Model and assumptions
Let \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) denote the performance that animal i would show under two diets. The average intervention effect is \(E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\). Only one potential outcome is observed for each animal. Random allocation can support estimating this contrast; an observational correlation \(\mathrm{cor}(X,Y)\) generally cannot.
For prediction, specify the target population and prediction time. Molecular measurements collected after the response occurs may help explain biology but cannot automatically support an earlier management decision.

4. Interpretation and scope
An integrated explanation remains a hypothesis unless the design and analysis support its causal interpretation. Tissue composition, environment, measurement error and reverse causation can produce associations. A smaller, well-designed set of measurements may answer the question better than an indiscriminate panel.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
A database record is not interchangeable with an organism, a sample or a gene. A study can contain many specimens, and a gene can have multiple transcripts and protein products. Sequence, expression, protein, structure and pathway resources answer different questions. Preserve species, genome assembly, accession/version, coordinate conventions and retrieval date alongside a record.
In a real project, select the organism and assembly before mapping variants to genes. Check whether a downloaded table reports gene IDs, transcript IDs, symbols or probes. Symbols can change or be shared. Joining on an ambiguous display label can duplicate rows or silently lose records. GEO, for example, distinguishes sample, series and platform records; these are different levels of metadata.

title: Biological databases and identifier mapping
text:
2. Model and assumptions
If feature f maps to several transcripts, a join produces several annotation rows for the same measured value. This is a representation of a relationship, not new biological replication. An eligible pathway background should be constructed from features that could have entered the analysis, after documenting the feature-to-gene mapping.
Check key uniqueness, unmatched records and row expansion before summarising. Define whether many features per gene will be combined, selected or retained; different choices answer different questions.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text: Distinguish sequence reads, assemblies, alignments and genotype calls; calculate simple quality and distance summaries; distinguish similarity from homology and association from mechanism.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Sequencing produces reads from molecules, not a finished genome. Assembly reconstructs sequence relationships; alignment compares reads or sequences against a reference; variant calling estimates differences under measurement and calling assumptions. Genotyping platforms measure selected variants. Genome assembly and annotation versions define the coordinates and biological interpretation.
A FASTA record stores a sequence with a header. FASTQ adds per-base quality information. A gap in an alignment represents an alignment decision about an insertion/deletion, not a fifth nucleotide. A SNP dosage of 0, 1 or 2 counts the stated allele in a diploid genotype and requires a missing-call convention.
Identity describes matching aligned residues. Homology describes common ancestry; it is not a percentage. Sequence similarity is evidence to interpret alongside length, complexity, significance and biological context.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For an aligned comparison with n comparable sites and k differences, \(p=k/n\) is the observed mismatch fraction. Under the Jukes–Cantor assumptions of equal base frequencies and equal substitution rates, \(d=-3/4\log(1-4p/3)\) estimates substitutions per site for \(p<3/4\). Alignment uncertainty and saturation limit this model.
For a Phred quality Q, the encoded error probability is \(10^{-Q/10}\). Summing these probabilities gives an expected number of errors, without assuming the errors are independent.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
Q <- c(10,20,30,40)
data.frame(Q=Q,error_probability=10^(-Q/10))


   Q error_probability
1 10             1e-01
2 20             1e-02
3 30             1e-03
4 40             1e-04


Show R code
a <- strsplit("ACGTACGTACGT","")[[1]]
b <- strsplit("ACGTTCGTTCGT","")[[1]]
p <- mean(a!=b)
d <- -.75*log(1-4*p/3)
c(observed_fraction=p, JC_distance=d)


observed_fraction       JC_distance 
        0.1666667         0.1884858 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(p-2/12)<1e-12, d>p)


The correction exceeds the observed difference because multiple changes can occur at a site. These short hypothetical sequences do not establish ancestry or a reliable divergence estimate.

title: Genomic measurements and sequence analysis
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Whole-genome workflows need species/reference selection, coverage, mapping and calling diagnostics, filtering and assessment of sampling. A clustering tree from distances is not automatically a species phylogeny. Review NCBI’s BLAST glossary for the distinction between identity and homology.

Why is the denominator comparable sites rather than all supplied characters?
Why can a dosage of 2 not be interpreted before specifying the counted allele?
Can a high-identity short alignment establish function?







Suggested answers






Gaps and unknown bases do not supply called nucleotide comparisons.
Two counts refer to a particular allele, not a universally favourable genotype.
No; coverage, complexity, evolutionary relationship and functional evidence matter.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text: Distinguish methylation proportions, chromatin-accessibility measurements and expression; evaluate coverage, tissue composition and regulatory claims.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Epigenomic assays measure selected properties of DNA and chromatin. Bisulfite-based methylation assays estimate methylated cytosines under conversion and mapping assumptions. Accessibility assays measure the representation of accessible regions under their own sampling process. Neither is a direct universal measure of gene activity. An epigenomic profile is tied to tissue, developmental stage, cellular composition and collection conditions.
Nutritional or environmental exposure can associate with a regulatory measurement. To claim an exposure causes a regulatory change, consider allocation and confounding; to claim that change mediates a phenotype, additional assumptions and evidence are needed. Genotype can affect both a regulatory measurement and the response. Sampling tissue after disease or production changes can also reverse the apparent direction of explanation.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A simple methylation summary is \(\widehat{p}=m/(m+u)\), where m and u are methylated and unmethylated reads at a supplied site. Under independent binomial sampling of reads conditional on a true proportion p, \(\mathrm{Var}(\widehat p)=p(1-p)/n\). This conditional measurement model does not describe all biological variability between animals; read depth is not the number of independent animals.
A pooled tissue proportion can change when cell-type proportions change even if methylation within each cell type remains constant.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
cell_methylation <- c(typeA=.2,typeB=.8)
composition <- rbind(control=c(.8,.2),treated=c(.3,.7))
pooled <- as.vector(composition %*% cell_methylation)
data.frame(group=rownames(composition), pooled_methylation=pooled)


    group pooled_methylation
1 control               0.32
2 treated               0.62


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(pooled[1]-.32)<1e-12, abs(pooled[2]-.62)<1e-12)
n <- c(10,100)
data.frame(reads=n,conditional_SE=sqrt(.5*.5/n))


  reads conditional_SE
1    10      0.1581139
2   100      0.0500000


The pooled proportion differs by .30 with no within-cell-type change. Increasing read depth reduces conditional sampling error, not the need for biological replication.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Conversion efficiency, assay specificity, mapping, coverage and cell composition need evaluation. Conventional bisulfite signals do not by themselves separate every cytosine modification. Technical proportions and production traits can be associated without a direct regulatory mechanism. Sequence and assay context must accompany an epigenomic coordinate.

title: Epigenomic measurements and regulatory interpretation
text:
5. Exercises

Did either cell type change methylation in the example?
Does sequencing one animal 100 times create 100 treatment replicates?
How could sampling time affect a regulatory interpretation?







Suggested answers






No; the mixture changed.
No; these are measurements of one animal, not independent allocations.
A profile measured after a phenotype changes can reflect its consequences rather than its antecedent causes.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text: Distinguish analytical features from confirmed metabolites; evaluate internal standards and scaling; separate concentration changes from relative signal differences.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text: Distinguish analytical features from confirmed metabolites; evaluate internal standards and scaling; separate concentration changes from relative signal differences.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Metabolomics measures small molecules using platforms with different coverage and selectivity. A detected feature may describe a mass/charge and retention-time signal rather than a confidently identified compound. Adducts, isotopes and fragments can yield multiple features associated with one molecule. Conversely, co-eluting compounds can complicate a signal.
Targeted assays can quantify defined compounds with calibrations; untargeted assays often yield relative intensities with varying identification confidence. Processing should document blanks, technical QC samples, drift, batches, detection limits and normalization. A table heading called concentration does not turn an arbitrary instrument signal into an absolute chemical measurement.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
2. Model and assumptions
If the observed signal is \(x_{ij}=a_j c_{ij}\) and an internal standard has known concentration \(c_s\) and the same multiplicative factor \(a_j\), the ratio \(x_{ij}/s_j\) cancels that factor. This works only to the extent that the standard tracks the relevant measurement process.
Scaling a feature to mean zero and variance one changes its contribution to a multivariate analysis. It does not convert arbitrary units into comparable concentrations.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
concentration <- c(2,3,4)
drift <- c(.8,1.1,1.4)
signal <- concentration*drift
standard <- 5*drift
ratio <- signal/standard
data.frame(concentration,signal,standard,ratio)


  concentration signal standard ratio
1             2    1.6      4.0   0.4
2             3    3.3      5.5   0.6
3             4    5.6      7.0   0.8


Show R code
stopifnot(max(abs(5*ratio-concentration))<1e-12)


The common drift cancels in this deliberately idealised example. If the analyte and standard respond differently to preparation or the instrument, that cancellation will be incomplete.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Chemical identity should have documented supporting evidence; a feature ID is not a metabolic pathway assignment. Avoid counting several signals from the same compound as independent confirmations. See the EMBL-EBI metabolite-identification lesson for the distinction between a detected signal and an assigned compound.

title: Metabolite features, identification and quantification
text:
5. Exercises

Why is a feature ID insufficient for a pathway claim?
Under what assumption does the standard correction work?
Why can unit-variance scaling amplify noisy features?







Suggested answers






The compound may not be established; mass, retention and additional chemical evidence need evaluation.
Analyte and standard share the specified multiplicative response.
Each retained feature is given similar variance weight, even when its original variation reflects measurement noise.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text: Define phenotypes and units; distinguish repeated observations from independent animals; align sensor measurements to biological sampling and decision times.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Phenomics can describe production, behaviour, physiology and environmental response across animals and time. Sensors create dense records, but the biological quantity still needs definition. A daily average, total, slope and within-day variability answer different questions. Document units, calibration, missing coverage and the interval represented by each summary.
When aligning a molecular sample with sensor data, decide whether the intended feature is a pre-sampling baseline, concurrent response or future outcome. A model for day-30 prediction cannot use day-45 sensor records at deployment. Aggregation can also hide short-lived events and differences in monitoring duration.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For animal i observed at \(n_i\) times, \(\bar y_i=\sum_t y_{it}/n_i\) is a mean over those recorded times, not necessarily the mean over the entire target period. Missing times need a coverage policy.
Under equal marginal variance \(\sigma^2\) and equal within-animal correlation \(\rho\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar y_i)=\sigma^2[1+(n_i-1)\rho]/n_i\). Additional correlated records improve precision more slowly than independent records.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
n <- c(1,5,20)
rho <- .6
variance <- (1+(n-1)*rho)/n
data.frame(records=n,variance_of_mean=variance)


  records variance_of_mean
1       1             1.00
2       5             0.68
3      20             0.62


Show R code
set.seed(1101)
records <- data.frame(animal=rep(c("a1","a2","a3"),each=5),
 day=rep(1:5,3), value=rep(c(8,10,12),each=5)+rnorm(15,sd=.4))
aggregate(value~animal,subset(records,day<=3),mean)


  animal     value
1     a1  7.726248
2     a2 10.086693
3     a3 12.094211


The variance approaches the correlation component rather than zero as repeated records accumulate. The summary intentionally uses days 1–3, demonstrating a defined time window.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
The equal-correlation model is a teaching simplification; actual serial correlation, drift, unequal coverage and animal-level variation need appropriate modelling. Neither millions of sensor rows nor precise technology automatically establish millions of experimental units.

title: Phenomics, sensors and measurement timing
text:
5. Exercises

What happens to variance when rho is zero?
Why should each animal’s monitoring coverage be reported?
Which records are eligible for a prediction made on day 3?







Suggested answers






It is sigma squared divided by n.
Means from different windows or selective missing times may not be comparable.
Information observed by day 3; later records are eligible only as outcomes or in a different task.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text: Define marker dosage and phenotype contrasts; identify confounding and linkage disequilibrium; distinguish GWAS, eQTL, TWAS, fine-mapping and prediction.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
GWAS evaluates association between variants and a phenotype. An eQTL analysis evaluates association between variants and expression. TWAS uses expression-related genetic information in a trait-association framework. These approaches connect measurements, but none automatically identifies a causal variant, causal gene or mediation mechanism.
Relatedness and population structure can induce association when genetic groups differ in environment or phenotype. Linkage disequilibrium allows a marker to tag nearby variation; multiple correlated associations need not imply multiple mechanisms. Fine-mapping compares candidate explanations under an explicit model and requires appropriate LD, coverage, allele alignment and prior assumptions. A posterior probability is conditional on that model and supplied candidates.
Genomic prediction evaluates the ability to predict new animals, rather than selecting the smallest association p-value. The deployment population and training relationships determine the relevant validation design.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A basic unrelated-sample model is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_g g_i+\gamma^T c_i+e_i\), where \(g_i\) counts a stated allele and c contains prespecified covariates. Residual independence and the design matter. With correlated relatives, a mixed-model or other suitable framework is needed.
For two marker vectors, their correlation describes association of the supplied dosages. It does not establish ancestry, phase, a causal allele or a calibrated fine-mapping probability.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1301)
ancestry <- rep(c(0,1),each=20)
g <- rbinom(40,2,ifelse(ancestry==0,.2,.8))
y <- 3*ancestry+rnorm(40)
unadjusted <- lm(y~g)
adjusted <- lm(y~g+ancestry)
c(unadjusted_marker=coef(unadjusted)["g"],adjusted_marker=coef(adjusted)["g"])


unadjusted_marker.g   adjusted_marker.g 
         1.44495380         -0.02545743 


Show R code
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(adjusted))$rank==3)
plot(g,y,col=ifelse(ancestry==0,"#1b9e77","#d95f02"),pch=19,
 xlab="Counted-allele dosage",ylab="Hypothetical phenotype")









The generating model contains no direct marker effect. Group differences can nevertheless create a marginal marker association. One realization does not make the adjusted estimate exactly zero.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Adjustment can reduce specified confounding but cannot guarantee that all confounding has been measured. Do not infer causality from conditional association, a TWAS signal or agreement between assays. Fit and validate appropriate models before applying any teaching formula to related livestock data.

title: Association, prediction and regulatory evidence
text:
5. Exercises

Why can a variant associate with a trait without changing it?
What is the eQTL response variable?
Why can randomly splitting relatives exaggerate deployment performance?







Suggested answers






LD with causal variation or association with ancestry/environment can produce the signal.
A specified expression measurement in a stated tissue/context.
Close relatives in training and test can make the task easier than prediction in a new family or population.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text: Distinguish early, intermediate and late integration; align samples and scales; evaluate common latent patterns, missing layers and validation.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Integration combines evidence across measurements to answer a defined question. Early integration concatenates compatible features before analysis. Intermediate strategies construct joint representations or relate layer-specific representations. Late integration combines outputs such as predictions or evidence summaries. Choice depends on matching, sample size, measurement process and the biological task.
Verify animal identity, specimen and time before computing cross-layer associations. Samples from the same animal but different time points are not automatically interchangeable. A missing layer can depend on disease severity or technical failure, so a complete-case subset may not represent the target population. Feature scaling controls the influence of units and variance; block weighting also controls the influence of unequal feature counts.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
2. Model and assumptions
For layer matrices \(X_k\) with animals in rows, a simple concatenation is \(X=[w_1 Z_1,\ldots,w_K Z_K]\), where \(Z_k\) uses training-derived centering/scaling. Choosing \(w_k=1/\sqrt{p_k}\) gives each standardized block the same total marginal variance p-weight in training when it has \(p_k\) nonconstant features. It is a design choice, not a universally optimal integration method.
Correlated layers may share biology, batch effects or repeated measurements. Cross-layer agreement is not independent replication by default.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
set.seed(1501)
z <- rnorm(12)
A <- cbind(z+rnorm(12,sd=.2), z+rnorm(12,sd=.2))
B <- cbind(z+rnorm(12,sd=.3), rnorm(12), rnorm(12))
ZA <- scale(A); ZB <- scale(B)
combined <- cbind(ZA/sqrt(ncol(ZA)),ZB/sqrt(ncol(ZB)))
fit <- prcomp(combined,center=FALSE,scale.=FALSE)
c(A_total_variance=sum(apply(ZA/sqrt(2),2,var)),
 B_total_variance=sum(apply(ZB/sqrt(3),2,var)),
 PC1_fraction=fit$sdev[1]^2/sum(fit$sdev^2))


A_total_variance B_total_variance     PC1_fraction 
       1.0000000        1.0000000        0.7082201 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(sum(apply(ZA/sqrt(2),2,var))-1)<1e-12)


Each block has total marginal variance one, but the joint PCs still depend on covariance. The common latent variable was deliberately supplied; a principal component is not a discovered mechanism.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
An integration example must specify the unit, timing, transformation, missingness policy, target and validation. The MultiAssayExperiment documentation illustrates explicit mappings between assay columns and biological subjects; these practicals implement small analogous checks with base R.

title: Integrating molecular layers and phenotypes
text:
5. Exercises

Why can a large feature block dominate concatenated PCA?
Does block weighting remove batch effects?
Where should scaling be estimated for prediction?







Suggested answers






More standardized features contribute more total variance.
No; weighting changes influence, not confounding.
Within each training split, then applied to held-out animals.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text: Document provenance and exclusions; distinguish access control from reproducibility; evaluate privacy, research integrity and responsible AI use.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
1. Biological question and measurements
Reproducibility means that the documented inputs and procedures can produce the reported analysis. It requires traceable data versions, sample definitions, transformations, software, random draws and model choices. A script that runs is only part of this record: excluded samples, manual corrections and selection decisions affect the result.
A public teaching example can use hypothetical data while a real collaboration may need controlled access. Genetic, ownership, location or linked production records can carry sensitive information. Permissions, consent or institutional agreements determine what may be shared; changing names alone does not necessarily prevent re-identification. Publish reusable methods and non-sensitive demonstrations without transferring restricted records into public repositories.
Responsible AI use includes identifying what the tool contributed and verifying code, citations and interpretations. Do not upload restricted data to an external service without the applicable authorisation. Specific governance decisions depend on the project’s agreements and local requirements.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
2. Model and assumptions
A manifest connects a file identifier, checksum, role and access category. A checksum can detect byte-level changes; it cannot determine whether a biological measurement or label is correct. Separate data provenance from biological validity.
An analysis record should distinguish prespecified decisions from exploratory choices and document deviations. Fixing a seed preserves one random realization; it does not establish that findings generalize.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
3. Worked example
The inputs below are hypothetical. Run the example, predict one change, then compare your prediction with the result. All executable code uses base R.


Show R code
path <- tempfile(fileext=".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(animal=c("fictional_a1","fictional_a2"),value=c(3,5)),
 path,row.names=FALSE)
manifest <- data.frame(role="hypothetical teaching input",checksum=unname(tools::md5sum(path)),
 access="public synthetic",unit="animal")
manifest


                         role                         checksum           access
1 hypothetical teaching input ca1fa9541bfb9f91c7a0cced0ac7f804 public synthetic
    unit
1 animal


Show R code
stopifnot(nchar(manifest$checksum)==32)
unlink(path) # Removes only the temporary file created in this example.


The manifest identifies bytes of one fictional teaching table. A different formatting or row order can change the checksum even when the scientific content is equivalent.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
4. Interpretation and scope
Keep credentials, private observations and restricted metadata out of public teaching sources. Report validation and limitations plainly, including null or inconsistent results. Reproducibility does not guarantee correct inference, responsible access or scientific validity.

title: Reproducibility, data governance and responsible research
text:
5. Exercises

Does an unchanged checksum certify correct animal identity?
What should be shared when data access is restricted?
Why record an exploratory feature-selection decision?







Suggested answers






No; it only certifies the same file bytes under the checksum mechanism.
Methods, metadata descriptions, access procedures and an appropriately non-sensitive example, subject to the governing agreements.
Selection affects uncertainty and replication; readers need to know how the analysis was chosen.
